content: A Pap smear is a microscopic examination of cells collected from the cervix, which is the lower part of the uterus that opens into the top of the vaginal canal. This test is primarily used as a screening tool for cervical cancer. How is the Pap smear performed? During the procedure, you will lie on an examination table and place your feet in stirrups. A healthcare provider will gently insert a speculum into the vagina to slightly open it, allowing them to visualize the vaginal canal and cervix. Cells are then carefully scraped from the cervical area using a small brush or spatula. These cells are sent to a laboratory for microscopic analysis. Who needs a Pap smear? The Pap smear is a critical screening test for cervical cancer. Routine Pap smears and pelvic examinations can help detect cervical cancer at an early stage. Screening should begin at age 21. After the initial test: Women should have a Pap smear every two years to check for cervical cancer. If you are over 30 years old and have had three consecutive negative Pap smears, your doctor may recommend testing every three years. If you or your sexual partner have new sexual partners, you should continue having a Pap smear every two years. After the age of 65–70, most women can stop having Pap smears if they have had three negative tests in the past 10 years. If you have a new sexual partner after age 65, you should resume Pap smear screening. Women who have had a total hysterectomy (removal of the uterus and cervix) and have no history of cervical dysplasia, cervical cancer, or other pelvic cancers may not need further Pap smears. How to prepare for a Pap smear? Before the test, inform your healthcare provider if you: Are taking any medications, including birth control pills. Have had an abnormal Pap smear in the past. Might be pregnant. To ensure accurate results, avoid the following for 24 hours before the test: Douching. Sexual intercourse. Taking a bath. Using tampons. Do not schedule your Pap smear during menstruation, as this may affect the accuracy of the test. However, if you are experiencing abnormal bleeding, your doctor may still recommend proceeding with the test. Additionally, empty your bladder just before the procedure. What to expect during the procedure? A Pap smear may cause mild discomfort, similar to menstrual cramps. You may also feel some pressure during the examination. Light bleeding or spotting may occur after the test. Where to find centers that perform Pap smears? You can consult your healthcare provider or local hospital for directions to facilities that perform Pap smears. What to expect (Outlook/Prognosis)? The Pap smear is not 100% accurate, and in rare cases, cervical cancer may be missed. However, cervical cancer typically develops very slowly, and follow-up Pap smears can detect concerning changes in time for effective treatment. Inform your doctor about all medications you are taking, as some, including estrogen and progestins, may influence the test results. Results: Normal Results: A normal (negative) result indicates that no abnormal cells are present. Note that normal value ranges may vary slightly between laboratories. Discuss the specific meaning of your test results with your doctor. Abnormal Results: Abnormal results are categorized as follows: ASCUS or AGUS (Atypical Squamous or Glandular Cells of Uncertain Significance): These changes may be due to an HPV infection but could also indicate precancerous changes. LSIL (Low-Grade Dysplasia) or HSIL (High-Grade Dysplasia): These findings suggest the presence of precancerous changes, with a higher risk of cervical cancer associated with HSIL. Carcinoma in Situ (CIS): This indicates abnormal changes that are likely to progress to cancer if left untreated. ASC-H (Atypical Squamous Cells, Cannot Exclude HSIL): This suggests abnormal changes that may be consistent with HSIL. AGC (Atypical Glandular Cells): These changes may indicate precancerous conditions in the upper cervical canal or inside the uterus. If abnormal changes are detected, further testing or follow-up is required. The next steps depend on the Pap smear results, your previous history of Pap smears, and your risk factors for cervical cancer. These steps may include: Colposcopy-directed biopsy: A closer examination of the cervix using a special magnifying instrument. HPV testing: To check for the presence of high-risk HPV types that are most likely to cause cervical cancer. For minor cell changes, doctors often recommend repeating the Pap smear in 3–6 months.
